items.abstract: <jats:p>Actuator failure on a remotely deployed robot results in decreased efficiency or even renders it inoperable. Robustness to these failures will become critical as robots are required to be more independent and operate out of the range of repair. To address these challenges, we present two approaches based on modular robotic architecture to improve robustness to actuator failure of both fixed-configuration robots and modular reconfigurable robots. Our work uses modular reconfigurable robots capable of modifying their style of locomotion and changing their designed morphology through ejecting modules. This framework improved the distance travelled and decreased the effort to move through the environment of simulated and physical robots. When the deployed robot was allowed to change its locomotion style, it showed improved robustness to actuator failure when compared to a robot with a fixed controller. Furthermore, a robot capable of changing its locomotion and design morphology statistically outlasted both tests with a fixed morphology. Testing was carried out using a gazebo simulation and validated in multiple tests in the field. We show for the first time that ejecting modular failed components can improve the overall mission length.</jats:p>
title: Enabling robustness to failure with modular field robots

items.abstract: Background: Generative AI can alter the surface form, fluency, rhetorical organisation, and evidential register of a health claim without necessarily changing its underlying proposition. High original-text accuracy therefore does not establish model robustness to claim-preserving rewriting, introducing a critical vulnerability into automated public health infrastructure and personalised digital health tools. Objective: To quantify how ChatGPT-based neutral, ELM central-route, and ELM peripheral-route transformations alter health-misinformation detector performance, computational persuasion features, and detector failure mechanisms, and to evaluate whether transformation-aware training mitigates detector failures and improves the reliability of automated health-information assessment. Methods: COVID-19 FNIR and Monkeypox corpora were evaluated under a paired C0–C3 design using four classical and five CNN/recurrent detectors. A balanced 200-root intervention cohort was generated with one C1–C3 descendant per condition. For mitigation, each dataset's intervention roots were divided into 50 augmentation roots and 50 untouched mitigation-test roots; C0-only augmentation was compared with C0+C1–C3 transformation-aware augmentation. Results: Across the initial intervention panel, macro-F1 fell from 0.987 to 0.428–0.479 on FNIR and from 0.922 to 0.731–0.781 on Monkeypox. Failure modes differed sharply, revealing distinct information-quality risks relevant to digital health safeguards. FNIR failure was dominated by false-positive inflation, indicating a risk of incorrectly flagging reliable health information, whereas mpox showed substantial increases in misinformation false negatives, indicating a risk of failing to identify rewritten misleading claims. Transformation-aware training increased mean C1–C3 macro-F1 on unseen Monkeypox roots by 0.148 across nine models (9/9 improved; Wilcoxon p=0.0039) while preserving panel-level C0 performance (+0.004). FNIR mitigation was smaller and heterogeneous (+0.035; 7/9 models improved; p=0.164), and cross-dataset transfer was inconsistent. Conclusions: Generative-AI rewriting produced substantial, dataset-dependent deterioration in health-misinformation detector performance, even under transformation instructions intended to preserve the underlying claims. Transformation-aware augmentation improved in-domain robustness, particularly for mpox, but did not consistently generalise across datasets. These findings support the inclusion of transformation-based stress testing and class-specific error analysis when evaluating potential automated health-information safeguards. Independent semantic-fidelity validation and application-specific evaluation remain necessary before clinical deployment implications can be established.
title: Generative-AI Rewriting and the Robustness of Health Misinformation Detection: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation of Failure Mechanisms and Mitigation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Swarm robotics addresses the design, deployment, and analysis of large groups of robots that collaborate to perform tasks in a decentralized manner. Research in this field has predominantly relied on simulations or small-scale robots with limited sensing, actuation, and computational capabilities. Consequently, despite significant advancements, swarm robotics has yet to see widespread commercial or industrial application. A major barrier to practical deployment is the lack of affordable, modern, and robust platforms suitable for real-world scenarios. Moreover, a narrow definition of what swarm robotics should be has restricted the scope of potential applications. In this paper, we argue that the development of more advanced robotic platforms—incorporating state-of-the-art technologies such as SLAM, computer vision, and reliable communication systems—and the adoption of a broader interpretation of swarm robotics could significantly expand its range of applicability. This would enable robot swarms to tackle a wider variety of real-world tasks and integrate more effectively with existing systems, ultimately paving the way for successful deployment.</jats:p>
title: Towards applied swarm robotics: current limitations and enablers

items.abstract: <jats:p>This book chapter delves into the transformative potential of emerging technologies, namely artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), in the field of mechanical engineering. It explores how these technologies are reshaping manufacturing processes, enabling autonomous systems, and fostering the development of smart products and intelligent machinery. The chapter emphasizes the integration of AI algorithms, machine learning, and data analytics as key drivers in enhancing efficiency, optimizing performance, and enabling predictive maintenance in mechanical engineering applications. In the section on AI in Mechanical Engineering, we provide an overview of AI and its applications, highlighting its pivotal role in automating manufacturing processes, thereby increasing productivity. We discuss AI-driven design optimization and intelligent decision-making in mechanical systems, along with AI-enabled predictive maintenance to enhance system reliability and reduce downtime.</jats:p>
